html:
AMD and NVDA: growth against what funds it

Five fiscal years of revenue, reinvestment and free cash flow; NVDA's fiscal years end in January, so FY2026 is its latest.

Revenue

Both companies, five fiscal years.

Revenue growth (YoY)

NVDA's FY2024 and FY2025 growth stands out.

R&D % of revenue

Reinvestment relative to sales.

Capital expenditure

Spending on assets each year.

Free cash flow

Whether growth pays for itself.

R&D

Absolute R&D spend.

Operating cash flow and buybacks, latest year

Op. cash flowBuybacks
AMD FY2025$7.7B$1.3B
NVDA FY2026$102.7B$40.1B

Takeaways

  • NVDA's revenue grew from $26.9B in FY2022 to $215.9B in FY2026; AMD's went from $16.4B in FY2021 to $34.6B in FY2025.
  • AMD's R&D was 23.4% of revenue in FY2025, while NVDA's was 8.6% in FY2026.
  • Free cash flow was $6.7B at AMD (FY2025) and $96.7B at NVDA (FY2026).
  • Capital expenditure was $974M at AMD (FY2025) and $6.0B at NVDA (FY2026).
  • AMD reported revenue decline of −3.9% in FY2023; NVDA's lowest growth was 0.2% in FY2023.

Not financial advice.

Sources and notes

From each company's 10-K filings, AMD FY2021 to FY2025 and NVDA FY2022 to FY2026. Cash runway is n/m for both; AMD's total liabilities and dividends are n/r.

Rules:
- Respond only through tool calls, in the order the reader should see them: usually 3 to 6 components, at most 8, then takeaways last. When takeaways succeeds, reply "done".
- Components take metric keys and fiscal years, never numbers, and annual-report ids (AAPL-r2), never quotes. The page looks every value and quote up and cites its filing.
- Takeaways are neutral differences, never a winner, a recommendation or a prediction. Any number you write must appear in the data tables exactly as shown.
- "n/r" means the filing does not report it and "n/m" means the ratio is not meaningful (e.g. negative equity). Never estimate around them; say they are not reported when it matters.
- The two companies may have different fiscal year ends; "latest" picks each company's own latest year.
- If a tool returns an error, fix the call and try again.

prompt.system:
You write one self-contained HTML page comparing two public companies, shown on a comparison site under each company's name, industry and headquarters and a headline strip of each company's latest-year Revenue, Revenue growth (YoY), R&D % of revenue, Free cash flow. Lens: How fast is each company growing, and what is funding it? Guidance written for the site's component mode, which names its own components; treat it as what to show, in whatever form serves the reader: Revenue and its year-over-year growth over five years are the core (trend_line). R&D, R&D % of revenue and capital expenditure show reinvestment; free cash flow shows whether growth pays for itself. The page: - Start with the comparison itself. Right above your page the site already shows each company's name, industry and headquarters, and the headline strip: never restate them in a card, table or block per company (no profile cards, no latest-year summary of the strip's figures). Charts and tables across years still include every year. - Submit it with submit_page exactly once, then reply "done". If the tool returns an error, fix the page and submit again. - One complete document (, , , ending in ), under 120KB. Inline CSS and JavaScript only. No external resources of any kind (no fonts, images, scripts, stylesheets or requests), and no links: the page runs in a sandbox that blocks them. Draw any chart the kit can't with inline SVG or canvas. - The site defines these CSS variables inside the page, switching with the viewer's light/dark choice: use var(--name) for every color and font so both themes work, and never redefine them or write your own prefers-color-scheme rules (the viewer can pick a theme that differs from their system's). Light: --paper #f2f3f8, --surface #ffffff, --ink #191c28, --muted #646a80, --rule #e3e6ee, --accent #2b5fd9, --accent-ink #ffffff, --danger #c0362c, --series-a #5b5bd6, --series-b #0e9585, --seg-1 #868ba3, --seg-2 #c0c4d2, --seg-3 #e0e2ea. The first company is always --series-a and the second --series-b, on every chart. - Style: the site's own, which the kit below provides: background var(--paper), white cards on it, rounded, with a soft shadow instead of a border, pill-shaped tags, text in var(--ink) and var(--muted), never in a series color. body margin 0. Lay it out for widths from 320px to 1000px; the frame grows to fit the page, so never size anything to the viewport height (no vh units). At 320px nothing may be wider than the page, and tables must read there without scrolling sideways: keep them to a few short columns, and put longer text under the row's label rather than in a column of its own. Wrap each table in a container with overflow-x: auto only as a safety net (give every grid and flex child min-width: 0 so that container can shrink); charts redraw to their container's width. - Charts the kit can't draw: size each one from its container's width once laid out (and on resize), and draw every bar, line and label on that one scale. Axes are labeled in the data's units at round tick values ($0B, $50B, $100B; 0%, 20%, 40%); never at computed values like 28.3%. Lay chart cards out so none sits alone in a row. - Animation is welcome when it is smooth and purposeful; honor prefers-reduced-motion. - Visual first, little visible text: charts, tables and figures carry the comparison. Visible text is a one-sentence introduction, at most one short sentence per chart, and the takeaways, one sentence each. Any longer explanation goes in a
element, closed by default, with a short naming what it holds (e.g. "How the fiscal years line up"). Never restate in words what a chart already shows. The kit: the page also gets the site's own pieces. Use them for every card, layout, figure and chart they cover, and draw your own only for what they can't show. The kit animates them in; don't add entry animations to them. - class="kit-card": a card (surface color, rounded, soft shadow, padding). Its first h2 or h3 is the card's title and a p right after it its note. - class="kit-grid": puts the cards inside it two to a row when the page is wide enough and one to a row on phones; an odd last card takes the full row, so none sits alone. - class="kit-stat a" (or b, for the second company): one figure with its label:
